overview.body:
**Meru** (*meru*) ​— The ‌Axis Mountain, ‌Olympus of ​the Hindus · ​Name of ​a fabulous ​mountain — ​the central point ‌of Jambūdvīpa, ​round which ​the sun, ‌moon and planets ​revolve — ‌belongs to ​the Sanskrit ‌tradition, where it ​is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Cosmic ​Mountain, Axis Mundi". ​The name ‌means "Name ​of a ‌fabulous mountain — ​the central ‌point of ​Jambūdvīpa, round ‌which the sun, ​moon and ‌planets revolve; ​the Olympus ​of Hindu mythology ‌and abode ‌of the ‌gods."[^1].

**Meru** ​is the world’s ​axle: the ‌golden mountain ​at the ​centre of the ‌cosmos, around ​which the ​sun, moon, ‌and planets revolve, ​on whose ‌summit Indra’s ​city stands, ​and whose four ​faces of ​gold, crystal, ‌ruby, and ‌lapis feed the ​four great ‌rivers of ​the directions. ​Every Indian cosmology ‌— Hindu, ‌Buddhist, Jain ‌— puts ‌Meru in the ​middle; every ‌mandala is ​its plan.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores the ​name as ‌**Meru** and ​serves its ​temple at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/meru/). The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a description computed ​from the ‌displayed form ​itself. The ‌plain ASCII form ​*meru* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by the ‌early domain-name ​system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**मेरु**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"Name ‌of ​a fabulous ​mountain ‌— ​the central ‌point ​of ‌Jambūdvīpa, round ​which ​the sun, ​moon ​and ​planets revolve; ‌the ​Olympus ‌of Hindu ​mythology ‌and ​abode of ‌the ​gods."[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form ​*meru* ‌survives only ‌because ‌the early ​domain-name ​system ‌could not ​carry ​diacritics; ‌it is ​a ​technological ‌compromise, not ​an ‌ancient ​spelling. The ​Unicode ​restoration ​**Meru** recovers ‌the ‌full ​diacritic detail ‌of ​the scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly ‌in the ‌address ‌bar. ​The restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— a ​description ‌computed ​from the ​displayed ​form ‌itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ​**m** ‌→ ​**M** — ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**e** → ​**e** ‌— ‌Same
- **r** ​→ ​**r** ​— Same
- ​**u** ‌→ ‌**u** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/ˈmɛruː/** ​— ​Sanskrit ​(IAST: Meru).[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Me-** — ​Short ‌e ​as in ‌“set”; ​the ​name ​is pre-Vedic ​in ​feel, ‌its etymology ​uncertain.
- ‌**-ru** ​— Long ‌ū ​as ‌in ​“rule”; the ‌name ​closes ​on the ‌resonant ‌liquid.
- ‌**** ​— The ​axis ‌mountain ​— the ​Olympus ‌of ​Hindu, Buddhist, ​and ‌Jain ​cosmology ‌alike.

For ​the ​modern ​speaker, the ​closest ‌approximation ‌is: “MEH-roo”

​Kindred ‌and ​historical ​forms of ‌the ‌name:

- ‌**Buddhist** — ‌Sumeru ​— ‌“excellent ​Meru”, the ​abode ​of ‌the thirty-three ​gods
- ​**Jain** ​— Meru ‌as ​the ​central ​peak of ‌the ​middle ‌world

All ​three ‌Indian ​religions ‌share Meru ‌— ​the ​one mountain ​in ​the ‌centre of ‌every ​map.

domains.body:
**Meru** ​is the ‌world’s ‌axle: the ​golden ​mountain at ​the ​centre of ​the ‌cosmos, around ​which ​the sun, ‌moon, ​and planets ‌revolve, ​on whose ‌summit ​Indra’s city ​stands, ​and whose ​four ​faces of ‌gold, ​crystal, ‌ruby, and ​lapis ‌feed the ​four ‌great rivers ​of ‌the directions. ​Every ​Indian cosmology ‌— ‌Hindu, Buddhist, ‌Jain ​— puts ​Meru ‌in the ​middle; ​every mandala ‌is ​its plan.[^1]

### ​The ‌Axis

The ​world ‌turns on ​Meru; ​the pole ​star ​wheels above ‌its ‌summit as ​the ‌heavens’ nail-head.

### ​The ​Four Faces

‌Gold ‌to the ‌east, ‌crystal south, ​ruby ‌west, lapis ​north ​— the ​four ‌colours ​of the ​mandala.

### ​City of ‌the ​Gods

Indra’s ​Amarāvatī ​crowns the ‌summit; ​the thirty-three ‌gods ​feast in ‌its ​halls.

### The ‌Mandala’s ‌Map

Every ​maṇḍala ​diagrams Meru: ​centre, ​four gates, ‌and ‌the enclosing ​world-rings.

mythology.body:
Meru’s mythology ​is cosmography — ‌the mountain’s biography is ‌the world’s architecture. ​It rises from ​the centre of ​Jambudvīpa, the rose-apple continent; ​the sun’s chariot ​circles it daily; ‌the Ganges falls ​first on its summit ​and only then ‌to the earth; ​and the gods’ wars ‌are fought on ​its terraces. The ‌Purāṇic geographies measure ​all distance from its ​base.[^1]

### The Mountain ​of Measure (Purāṇic ​Cosmography)

The Purāṇas ​give Meru its statistics: ‌84,000 leagues high, ​its base 32,000 ‌across, its summit ​the square of the ‌gods’ city. The ​sun’s horses, tired ‌from circling it, ​rest at night on ‌its western face; ​the moon’s waxing ​is the gods’ ‌drinking of the lunar ‌soma on its ‌terraces. The mountain ​is the cosmos’s clock, ​scale, and sceptre.[^2]

### ‌The River’s First ​Fall (Gangā Cycle)

​When Bhagīratha won the ‌Ganges’ descent for ​his burned ancestors, ​the river fell ‌first from heaven onto ​the matted hair ‌of Śiva — ​and before that, ​the tradition adds, upon ​Meru’s summit, where ​the gods’ gardens ‌divided her into ‌the seven streams. Meru ​is the river’s ‌first landing, heaven’s ​customs-house.

### The Mountain Diagrammed ​(Mandala Theology)

The ‌Buddhist and Hindu ‌maṇḍala is Meru ‌flattened into a map: ‌the square’s four ​gates are its ‌faces, the inner ​palace the summit’s city, ​the concentric rings ​its seven world-encircling ‌ranges. To construct ​a mandala is to ​rebuild Meru; to ​enter it is ‌to climb. The ​Vajrayāna made the diagram ​the path itself.

### ​The Churning’s Spindle ‌(Samudra Manthana)

When ​the gods and demons ‌churned the ocean ​of milk, the ‌churning-rod was Mandara, Meru’s ​little brother of ‌a mountain; the ‌serpent Vāsuki the ​rope. Meru’s family thus ​supplied the axis ​of the gods’ ​greatest work — ‌the axis-mountain’s line, lending ‌itself to every ​cosmic rotation.

vedic-references.body:
The Vedas, the oldest stratum of Sanskrit scripture, contain hymns and litanies that name or allude to Meru. Ṛgvedic, Yajurvedic, and Atharvavedic passages establish the figure's early association with cosmic mountain.

The IAST restoration Meru marks the scholarly transliteration of those Vedic passages.[^1]

upanishads.body:
The Upaniṣads shift the focus from ritual to metaphysics, reinterpreting divine names as symbols of ultimate reality. Meru appears or is implied in passages that map the pantheon onto the self and the cosmos.

The restored form Meru carries the diacritic precision of Sanskrit scholarship.[^1]

puranas.body:
The Purāṇas narrate the myths, genealogies, and iconographies of Meru in encyclopedic Sanskrit compendia. Texts such as the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Śiva Purāṇa, and Devībhāgavata Purāṇa shape the devotional identity of the figure.

The IAST form Meru is the scholarly anchor across these compendia.[^1]

mantras.body:
Mantras and stotras addressed to Meru encode the name in ritual sound, often accompanied by visualizations and offerings. The syllabic structure of Sanskrit lends itself to sonic veneration.

The restored spelling Meru preserves the precise phonetic value used in recitation and scholarly citation.[^1]
